narrative:
The model estimates you have a 13% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, zero failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of traits the model sees the absence of prior setbacks as a warning sign rather than a strength. 

The second strongest influence is your clear desire to pursue higher education. This works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing, which makes sense because every student who succeeded also wanted to continue studying.

Third, your reason for choosing this school—being close to home—also nudges the outcome slightly toward passing. Most successful students chose the school for its course offerings or reputation rather than location, so your choice is less common among those who ultimately passed.

To improve, focus on building consistent study habits beyond your current pattern of less than two hours per week, which is lower than most students who succeeded. Consider using the internet access you currently lack, reducing time spent going out with friends, and seeking extra academic support even though you do not have it now. These small changes can strengthen the positive signals the model already sees in your ambition for higher education.
